header: Date: 2027-09-21 | Start: 15:00 PDT | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Reyes (Peregrine CTO), Sana Malik (Lead ML Eng), Ethan Ford (SRE)
summary: Discovery focused on p95 latency targets and throughput for Peregrine's conversational and batch workloads. Peregrine is evaluating Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Key constraints: p95 targets (chat <= 350ms ideally, long-form batch p95 <= 1s), sustained concurrency ~200-500, streaming support, and token/sec benchmarking for 4-8k window models. Action: send benchmarking template and set technical deep-dive to run pilot on Dedicated.
topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
transcript:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we've got about 45 minutes, quick intros?
[00:08] Jordan (Peregrine CTO): Jordan here, I'm the CTO, we run the inference stack and own latency SLOs.
[00:12] Sana (Lead ML Eng): Sana, lead ML, I'm focused on model quality and perf.
[00:15] Ethan (SRE): Ethan, SRE, infra and cost ops.
[00:18] Maya (Redwood SE): Maya here, I'll go into the token/sec and p95 details.
[00:22] Alex (Redwood AE): Awesome. Quick agenda: understand your p95 targets, concurrency, streaming needs, and then map Hosted/Dedicated/Private options.
[00:30] Jordan: high level — our primary use case is conversational assistant inside our product. For front-line UX we need p95 ideally under 350ms for short prompts (under 128 tokens), longer completions are ok up to 1s p95, and batch inference for analytics where throughput matters. We're running ~200-500 concurrent sessions during peak, roughly 20 tokens/sec per session average but bursty.
[00:50] Maya: okay that's helpful. when you say 20 tokens/sec per session, are you streaming to the user?
[00:54] Jordan: yes streaming for chat, we need token-by-token streaming — low tail latency is critical.
[00:59] Sana: we also have long context windows, many conversations go to 8k tokens, sometimes 32k for long docs. So the model size and KV cache behavior will matter.
[01:10] Alex: got it. Two axes: per-request p95 and sustained throughput (tokens/sec). For streaming the server-side p95 for first bytes is often the hard SLO. For Hosted, we optimize for fast cold-start and multi-tenant; Dedicated gives you reserved capacity to hit consistent p95 at scale; Private gives full control but ops overhead.
[01:32] Ethan: our concern is variability. Hosted is appealing but we need predictable tails for SLAs. Can Redwood guarantee p95 targets on Hosted, or do we need Dedicated?
[01:40] Maya: short answer — for predictable p95 at 200-500 concurrency we usually recommend Dedicated. Hosted can meet p95 for smaller workloads but as concurrency rises burst coldstart and noisy neighbors can push tails up. Dedicated gives controlled GPU pools, autoscaling, and pinned model variants.
[02:00] Jordan: what about streaming? We need token/sec rates measured end-to-end including network and client-side buffering.
[02:06] Maya: our benchmark approach measures: 1) first-byte latency (time to first token), 2) steady-state token latency, and 3) aggregate tokens/sec for a pool. We run synthetic workloads with your prompt distributions. For example earlier benchmarks for a 16k context 13B-style model showed p95 first-byte ~180–220ms on Dedicated with 8xA100 equiv under 300 concurrent streams. Token throughput around 150–500 tokens/sec per GPU depending on quantization and batching.
[02:40] Sana: those are promising. We use a mix of open weights and a couple proprietary fine-tuned models — how does Redwood handle model variants and fallback?
[02:48] Maya: we support pinned model versions and smart routing. If Dedicated capacity hits a limit you can route to a compatible hosted variant or a quantized version. We also have KV prefix caching to avoid re-encoding long histories — that helps p95 for chat. Note: sometimes transcript here has 'K V cash' in older notes, sorry typo.
[03:05] Ethan: on security we need VPC peering, KMS integration, and audit logs. Private would be ideal if we need air-gapped or strict residency.
[03:12] Alex: Redwood Private offers a customer-managed control plane and on-prem package; we integrate with KMS/HSM, SAML SSO, RBAC, and SOC2/ISO artifacts. Dedicated can be within your VPC for isolation too (VPC mode).
[03:28] Jordan: pricing tradeoff? Dedicated vs Hosted cost per token, roughly?
[03:33] Alex: Hosted is per-token; Dedicated is reserved capacity — higher baseline but lower unit cost at scale. We'll send a pricing sheet with example unit economics based on your concurrency and token/sec.
[03:45] Sana: for benchmarking we want to run our prompt sets — what's the recommended token/sec benchmarking methodology?
[03:50] Maya: we ask for three representative prompt sets: short chat (<=128 tokens), medium (128–2k), long context (8k–32k). We run: a) 95th-first-byte latency for streaming b) steady-state token latency c) sustained tokens/sec for N concurrent streams and for batch endpoints. We'll provide a template CSV and a harness to reproduce results.
[04:12] Jordan: can you give a ballpark: for p95 first-byte for short chat — Hosted vs Dedicated numbers?
[04:18] Maya: Hosted short-chat p95 often ~220–400ms depending on region and load. Dedicated typically ~150–250ms in similar conditions with reserved GPUs and tuned batching. For long context windows the difference can widen because of KV cache warmup and memory bandwidth.
[04:36] Ethan: concurrency 200–500 — that means how many GPUs? Any rule of thumb?
[04:40] Maya: rough rule: concurrency per GPU depends on model and batching. For a 13B-like model serving streaming, you might get ~50–120 concurrent low-latency streams per high-end GPU with careful batching and early-response optimizations. For your 200–500 concurrency, you'd look at a pool of ~4–10 high-end cards; Dedicated lets you size that predictably. We'll run exact sims in the pilot.
[04:58] Sana: token/sec per GPU also depends on quantization and kernels. If we quantize to int8 we see 1.5–2x throughput improvements vs fp16 in many cases. But regen quality matters.
[05:09] Maya: yes we recommend quantization experiments in Redwood Optimize; we surface model/quantization tradeoffs per workload.
[05:16] Jordan: for our pilot we want to validate p95 at peak and check cost. What's a minimal pilot footprint?
[05:22] Alex: typical pilot: 2–4 GPUs for 2 weeks with your prompts and traffic replay. For your scale I'd propose 4 GPUs with dedicated autoscaling and a synthetic load to get to 300 concurrency. That should surface p95 tails and QoS.
[05:36] Ethan: how do you handle KV cache across restarts? We need persistent cache to avoid re-computing history for long sessions.
[05:42] Maya: the runtime persists KV cache in memory per worker and supports warm-reuse; in Dedicated/Private we can configure sticky sessions and cache hot-resident keys. There's also automatic prefix caching for commonly repeated contexts. We'll include details in the tech doc.
[05:56] Sana: monitoring — we need token-level cost, p95 per-route, and alerting tied to regressions.
[06:02] Maya: Redwood Console provides per-route p50/p95 breakdown, token cost, traces, and can integrate with your alerts. For regressions we tie evals to prompt sets to detect quality drops.
[06:12] Jordan: any gotchas with streaming over mobile clients — jitter, network spikes?
[06:16] Alex: client-side buffering is often the biggest factor; server first-byte latency is necessary but not sufficient. We'll share best practices: small initial tokens, chunking, client ack patterns.
[06:27] Ethan: regarding compliance — we require SOC2 plus data residency in us-east for logs. Is that supported?
[06:32] Alex: yes, we have SOC2 reports and can host Dedicated in us-east. Private on-prem supports full residency. We'll include SOC2 artifacts in the security pack.
[06:41] Jordan: excellent. Can you run a checklist of what you need from us to run the pilot?
[06:45] Maya: we need: 1) prompt sets and representative traffic patterns 2) p95 SLOs for each set 3) sample models (weights or access details) 4) expected concurrency distribution 5) any network constraints (VPC peering)
[06:58] Jordan: Sana will send prompt sets and SLOs, Ethan will share infra telemetry and network constraints.
[07:04] Sana: yes I'll package them tonight.
[07:06] Alex: Great. Recap: Redwood to send benchmarking template, pricing, SOC2 + security pack, propose pilot (4 GPUs, 2 weeks). Customer to send prompt sets, SLOs, telemetry. We'll schedule a deep technical session next week.
[07:20] Ethan: one last quick question — can you do canary rollouts between quantized and full models to avoid regressions?
[07:25] Maya: yes we support canary/A-B rollouts and automatic fallback. We can route a small percentage to quantized model and monitor quality metrics.
[07:32] Jordan: thanks all. That covers it.
[07:36] Alex: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the docs and calendar invite.
[07:40] [call ends]

Notes: transcription includes occasional mis-attributions and small typos (e.g., 'K V cash' instead of KV cache). The transcript contains natural speech patterns, interruptions, and technical clarifications. The p95 numbers are preliminary and subject to pilot verification.
